entries.question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers state The Scarab God has no abilities while face down, so it doesn’t have a dies trigger when it dies during combat.
entries.answer:
No triggered ability fires. While The Scarab God is face down (turned face down by Ixidron's ability), it has none of its normal abilities — it's just a vanilla 2/2 creature, as Ixidron's own reminder text confirms ("turn all other nontoken creatures face down. (They're 2/2 creatures.)"). A face-down permanent's copiable values are reset to those of a generic 2/2 with no name, text, or abilities; only when it's turned face up do its printed abilities (including "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand at the beginning of the next end step") come back into play, and even then any turning-face-up ability only applies as it's turned face up, not retroactively [708.8], [708.11]. Since the permanent never turns face up here, it never regains its 'dies' trigger.

So in this combat: Archer's attacking face-down 2/2 (which is really The Scarab God) is blocked by Nia's Scathe Zombies (2/2). Combat damage is dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action [510.2], [703.4m], processed via the normal damage steps [120.4b], [120.4c]. If the face-down creature dies as a state-based action from that damage, it goes to the graveyard as a face-up card (losing 'face-down' status is a characteristic tied to being on the battlefield, so once it leaves the battlefield it's simply The Scarab God card in the graveyard) — but no 'dies' triggered ability ever fires, because at the moment it died it was a face-down permanent with no such ability, and abilities don't retroactively apply after the fact [708.8]. Note this would be different if some effect had already turned it face up before it died — then the real 'dies' trigger would exist and would trigger normally.

Bottom line: The Scarab God does not trigger its death ability in this scenario, because it's still face down (a blank 2/2) when combat damage resolves, and face-down permanents don't have that ability to trigger.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

entries.question: Aminah controls [Shapers' Sanctuary], [Spellskite], and [Feral Krushok]. Nico casts [Pyromatics] targeting Feral Krushok. Aminah activates Spellskite to change the target of Pyromatics to Spellskite. How many times does Shapers' Sanctuary trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Shapers' Sanctuary triggers twice—once when Pyromatics first targets Feral Krushok and again when Spellskite becomes the spell's target after the change.
entries.answer:
Shapers' Sanctuary triggers twice in this sequence. First, when Nico casts Pyromatics targeting Feral Krushok, Feral Krushok (a creature Aminah controls) becomes the target of a spell Nico (an opponent) controls, which is exactly the trigger condition on Shapers' Sanctuary's text: "Whenever a creature you control becomes the target of a spell or ability an opponent controls, you may draw a card." That's trigger #1.

Second, when Aminah activates Spellskite's ability — "{U/P}: Change a target of target spell or ability to this creature" — that ability changes the (single) target of Pyromatics from Feral Krushok to Spellskite, following the "change a target" process ([Change a Target], [115.7], [115.7b]). Once that change happens, Spellskite is now the target of Pyromatics, a spell controlled by Nico, an opponent. Spellskite is also a creature Aminah controls, so Shapers' Sanctuary's trigger condition ("a creature you control becomes the target of a spell or ability an opponent controls") is met again, independently of the first trigger. That's trigger #2.

Note that Spellskite's own ability is activated by Aminah, its controller, so it doesn't itself cause Shapers' Sanctuary to trigger (that would require an opponent's spell or ability); it's specifically Pyromatics — Nico's spell — re-targeting Spellskite that causes the second trigger. Each trigger is a separate instance of "you may draw a card," so Aminah gets two separate optional draws (per Shapers' Sanctuary ruling #0/#1, each of these triggers even resolves before Pyromatics itself resolves, giving Aminah a chance to act with each draw before the spell/ability that caused it resolves). This holds the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since the rules cited here (target-changing rules and the card's own trigger text) don't vary by player count — no multiplayer-specific rule changes how targeting or this trigger works.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Twice. Shapers' Sanctuary will trigger the first time when Pyromatics is initially cast targeting Feral Krushok.. Shapers' Sanctuary will trigger again when Spellskite becomes the target of the spell.

entries.question: Anderson plays their land for the turn, then casts a morphed [Zoetic Cavern]. Nataly casts [Delay] targeting Zoetic Cavern on the stack. After that resolves, Anderson casts [Timecrafting] to remove 2 time counters from Zoetic Cavern. After that resolves, Anderson casts Timecrafting to remove the last time counter from Zoetic Cavern. What happens to Zoetic Cavern?
entries.reason: The candidate leaves open that Anderson could play the suspended face-down creature "if able" and never applies the one-land-per-turn restriction, whereas the reference concludes it remains exiled because Anderson has already played a land this turn.
entries.answer:
Zoetic Cavern ends up exiled and hidden until Anderson decides (and is able) to play it again, and if he does it comes back as a face-down 2/2 creature with haste, not as the land — it only becomes the land again if Anderson later pays its morph cost to turn it face up.

Step by step:

1) When Anderson casts a morphed Zoetic Cavern, it becomes a face-down 2/2 creature spell with no name, text, subtypes, or mana cost on the stack (this is Zoetic Cavern's own "Morph {2}" ability combined with rule [702.37c]).

2) Nataly's Delay resolves, countering that spell. Delay's own text says the countered spell is exiled with three time counters instead of going to its owner's graveyard, and "if it doesn't have suspend, it gains suspend" — Zoetic Cavern doesn't have suspend, so it gains it (Delay). Crucially, rule [702.37c] says "The morph effect applies to the face-down object wherever it is, and it ends when the permanent is turned face up" — since nobody ever turns it face up, it stays face-down (2/2, no name/text/subtypes/mana cost) even after it moves into exile. Rule [406.3a] confirms that face-down cards can't be examined by other players except when instructions allow it, so this Zoetic Cavern sits in exile completely hidden, now suspended (exiled, has suspend, has a time counter — rule [702.62b]).

3) Anderson's first Timecrafting (X=2) removes 2 of the 3 time counters, leaving 1. It's still suspended.

4) Anderson's second Timecrafting (X=1) removes the last time counter. This triggers the third suspend ability [702.62a]: "When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it's exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. If you don't, it remains exiled. If you cast a creature spell this way, it gains haste until you lose control of the spell or the permanent it becomes." Because the card is currently a face-down object with "no mana cost," that cost requirement is trivially satisfied — Anderson may simply play it.

5) Since the face-down status persists (per [702.37c]), what's being played is still that 2/2 face-down creature, not the land Zoetic Cavern. If Anderson chooses to (and is able to), it's cast as that face-down creature spell; per [702.37c] it will resolve "with the same characteristics the spell had," i.e., as a face-down 2/2 creature permanent, and because it was cast as a creature spell via the suspend trigger, it gains haste until Anderson loses control of the spell or the permanent (suspend's own text, [702.62a]). At any later point Anderson may pay Zoetic Cavern's morph cost of {2} as a special action to turn it face up ([702.37e]), which would restore it to being the land Zoetic Cavern (with "{T}: Add {C}") and end the morph/haste situation.

If Anderson instead declines, or simply isn't able to play it at that moment, it "remains exiled" per the suspend ability's own text — still face-down, now with zero time counters, and no longer suspended per [702.62b] (suspended requires a time counter).

One timing note: I'm assuming Anderson is able to cast the creature spell at the moment the suspend trigger resolves (the provided rules don't include the general timing-restriction rules for casting creatures, so I can't confirm whether any outside restriction would stop him — but nothing in the given rules suggests it's blocked here). This is a two-player-style example; nothing here changes if there are more players at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It will remain in exile. Suspend allows Anderson to play it, but does not allow Anderson to play additional lands. Since they has already played their land for the turn, they cannot play Zoetic Cavern.

entries.question: Aubree controls an [Opal Acrolith] that is currently a creature and a [Sliver Construct]. They cast [Cytoshape] to turn the Sliver Construct into a copy of Opal Acrolith. Then they activate Sliver Construct's ability to turn it into an enchantment. What happens at the end of turn?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and reference conclude the Cytoshape copy ends at cleanup while the separate "becomes an enchantment" effect persists, leaving the permanent as a noncreature enchantment named Sliver Construct at end of turn.
entries.answer:
At the end of the turn, the permanent does NOT go back to being a 2/2 Artifact Creature — Sliver Construct — it ends the turn as a plain, noncreature Enchantment (named Sliver Construct again, with only Sliver Construct's own printed ability), because the "becomes an enchantment" effect Aubree triggered while it was a copy keeps applying even after the copy wears off.

Here's the full sequence:

1) Cytoshape resolves and Sliver Construct "becomes a copy of" Opal Acrolith. Opal Acrolith is only a 2/4 Soldier creature at that moment because of its own triggered ability's continuous effect, not because that's part of its printed/copiable characteristics — this is exactly analogous to the Cytoshape ruling about copying an animated Blinkmoth Nexus: "the printed wording will be copied" [Cytoshape ruling #0]. So Sliver Construct copies Opal Acrolith's printed form: card type Enchantment, mana cost {2}{W}, name "Opal Acrolith," and both of its abilities — it does NOT copy the temporary "is currently a creature" state. So immediately after Cytoshape resolves, the permanent is a noncreature Enchantment, not the 2/4 Soldier creature Aubree may have expected.

2) Aubree then activates the (now-copied) ability "{0}: This permanent becomes an enchantment." Per Opal Acrolith's own rulings, this effect makes "this permanent" no longer a creature [Opal Acrolith ruling #2] — which is already true here, so there's no visible change. But this activation creates its own distinct, ongoing continuous effect setting this specific permanent's type to Enchantment. Rule [700.7] confirms that an ability referring to "this permanent" keeps tracking that same object even as its characteristics change later.

3) At the cleanup step, Cytoshape's "until end of turn" copy effect expires, and "the creature reverts to what it was before" [Cytoshape ruling #6] — so the permanent's copiable values go back to Sliver Construct's own name, card types (Artifact Creature), and ability, and it loses Opal Acrolith's abilities entirely. However, rule [707.4] specifically states that when a permanent stops copying one object (here, reverting to itself), "this also doesn't change any noncopy effects presently affecting the permanent." The "becomes an enchantment" effect from step 2 is exactly such a noncopy effect, and it is still in effect — it isn't tied to Cytoshape's duration at all. So it keeps applying to the same object even though the ability that generated it (which only existed while the permanent was copying Opal Acrolith) is gone.

That leftover type-setting effect replaces the object's card types with just "Enchantment," and per rule [205.1a], since the Creature (and Artifact) types are gone, the correlated subtypes "Sliver" and "Construct" are removed too (they'd come back if it ever regains the creature type). Net result: the permanent ends the turn as a noncreature Enchantment called Sliver Construct, with only its own original ability, no power/toughness that matters (since it isn't a creature), and no Sliver or Construct subtypes — it does not revert to being a 2/2 creature.

This all happens on the battlefield without any zone change, so there's no "new object" reset involved. I'm assuming the events happen in the exact order given (cast Cytoshape, then activate the ability, then reach end of turn) — the question doesn't leave that order ambiguous, so no alternate-timing caveat is needed here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect making Sliver Construct a copy of Opal Acrolith ends, but the effect making it an enchantment does not. It's a noncreature enchantment named "Sliver Construct" with no abilities.

entries.question: Avery controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Evermind] on top of their library, can they cast it?
entries.reason: Both conclude that Evermind’s mana value is 0 so Bolas’s Citadel’s alternative life payment is 0 life, which can be paid, allowing Avery to cast it.
entries.answer:
Yes. Bolas's Citadel lets Avery cast spells from the top of their library, but instead of paying the spell's mana cost, Avery pays life equal to its mana value. Evermind has a mana value of 0, so the cost to cast it this way is 0 life — and rule [118.3b] explicitly states that players can always pay 0 life, since paying 0 of a required resource is always legal. Normally Evermind can't be cast on its own because it has no mana cost at all ([Evermind ruling #2] notes this, saying it needs an alternate means like Sunforger to be cast), but Bolas's Citadel's ability is itself an alternative cost (an additional/alternative cost is an ability of the card, per [113.2b]) that replaces the mana-cost payment with a life payment. Since that alternative cost is 0 life and 0 life is always payable, Avery is not blocked by rule [118.3] (can't pay a cost without the resources to pay it fully) — 0 is trivially payable. So Avery may cast Evermind off the top of their library via Bolas's Citadel, paying 0 life instead of a nonexistent mana cost.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Normally because Evermind has no mana cost it can't be cast. However Bolas's Citadel is casting it for an alternative cost, and therefore ignores the actual cost of the spell. When calculating the mana value of a spell with no mana cost it's considered zero.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Sidisi's Pet] on top of their library, can they cast it for its morph cost? If so, how much life will they pay?
entries.reason: The candidate permits using morph while Bolas's Citadel is active (paying {3} rather than life), which contradicts the correct ruling that morph is an alternative cost and cannot be combined with Bolas's Citadel's alternative cost.
entries.answer:
Yes — Autumn can cast Sidisi's Pet face down using its morph ability from the top of her library while she controls Bolas's Citadel, and she pays {3} generic mana for it, not life.

Here's why: Bolas's Citadel's static ability lets Autumn "cast spells from the top of your library," and morph is itself "a static ability that functions in any zone from which you could play the card it's on" [702.37a]. Since Bolas's Citadel gives permission to cast spells (of any type) from the top of the library, and casting Sidisi's Pet face down via morph still produces a spell (a 2/2 face-down creature spell with no name, text, subtypes, or mana cost) [702.37c], that permission covers casting it face down as well as face up.

Now for the cost. Morph is an alternative cost: "Morph [cost]" means "You may cast this card as a 2/2 face-down creature... by paying {3} rather than paying its mana cost" [702.37a][702.37c]. Alternative costs like this are paid instead of the mana cost [118.9b]. Bolas's Citadel's replacement ("pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost") only substitutes for paying the card's actual mana cost when you cast it that way. Because Sidisi's Pet's morph ability already replaces "paying its mana cost" with paying {3}, Autumn is not paying the mana cost at all in this line — she's paying the morph alternative cost. Rule 601.2b is explicit that "a player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell," so Bolas's Citadel's life-for-mana-value substitution and the morph {3} alternative cost don't stack; only the morph cost applies here.

So Autumn pays {3} (generic mana, not life) to cast Sidisi's Pet face down as a 2/2 with no name, text, subtypes, or mana cost. She does not pay any life for this cast, since Bolas's Citadel's life payment only kicks in when the mana cost itself would otherwise be paid [601.2f]. Later, at any time she has priority, she can turn it face up by paying its morph cost of {1}{B} as a special action that doesn't use the stack, per Sidisi's Pet's own text and [702.37e] and [Sidisi's Pet ruling #5][Sidisi's Pet ruling #3] — that's separate from casting it and unaffected by Bolas's Citadel.

This assumes she has no other alternative-cost effects in play that would also compete for the single alternative-cost slot; if some other effect also wanted to modify how she casts this spell, only one alternative method could apply per [601.2b].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, they can't cast it. If Autumn uses Bolas's Citadel to cast a spell, they are applying an alternative cost. Morph is also an alternative cost. Only one alternative cost can be applied to a spell when casting it.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Lovestruck Beast] on top of their library. Can they cast [Heart's Desire]? If so, how much life do they pay?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ashley can cast Heart's Desire from the top of the library thanks to Bolas's Citadel and that the life payment is equal to the spell's mana value, which is 1.
entries.answer:
Yes. Ashley may cast Heart's Desire (the Adventure side of Lovestruck Beast // Heart's Desire) directly off the top of their library because Bolas's Citadel grants permission to cast spells from that zone, and Ashley pays 1 life for it.

Bolas's Citadel reads, in part, "You may play lands and cast spells from the top of your library. If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." This is a static ability that lets Ashley cast a spell from a zone (the library) other than the hand, which is normally required to cast a spell (rule 601.3e requires some rule or effect to permit casting from a zone other than hand, and Bolas's Citadel provides exactly that permission). Casting a card is defined generically in rule 601.2b as taking it from wherever it is and putting it on the stack while paying its costs — it doesn't require the card to start in the hand, only that some rule or effect authorizes the cast from its current zone, which Bolas's Citadel does here.

Because Lovestruck Beast // Heart's Desire has two castable faces, and the card on top of the library can be cast as either the creature Lovestruck Beast or the sorcery Adventure Heart's Desire, Ashley may choose to cast Heart's Desire specifically. Bolas's Citadel's cost-substitution effect ("pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost") functions as an alternative cost under rule 118.9 — it replaces the mana cost, and that substituted cost is applied during cost determination per rule 601.2f, where alternative and additional costs are folded into the total cost before it locks in.

Heart's Desire's printed mana cost is {G} (one green mana, no generic component), so its mana value is 1. Therefore the life payment required by Bolas's Citadel is 1 life, not any amount of green mana — Ashley pays 1 life instead of {G}.

After Heart's Desire resolves, its own text exiles the card (per its Adventure reminder text), after which Lovestruck Beast could later be cast from exile in the normal way; that later cast would not go through Bolas's Citadel's top-of-library permission, since the card would no longer be on top of the library.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes and it will cost Ashley 1 life. As part of putting Lovestruck Beast on the stack Ashley chooses whether or not they want to cast the Adventure or not. If they casts Heart's Desire they will need to pay life equal to the mana value of the spell they are casting, which in this case is one.

entries.question: Angelique has [Copy Enchantment] enter the battlefield as a copy of [Estrid's Invocation], which is a copy of [Hardened-Scale Armor]. At the beginning of their next upkeep, which permanents may Angelique exile?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Copy Enchantment lacks the upkeep-exile ability (so nothing can be exiled), which contradicts the reference that both Copy Enchantment and Estrid's Invocation have the ability and may be exiled.
entries.answer:
Angelique's Copy Enchantment ends up as an exact copy of Hardened-Scale Armor — a plain Aura that says only "Enchant creature" and "Enchanted creature gets +3/+3." It does NOT gain Estrid's Invocation's "At the beginning of your upkeep, you may exile this enchantment..." ability. Since that ability simply doesn't exist on the resulting permanent, at the beginning of Angelique's next upkeep there is no such triggered ability to use, so Angelique may not exile anything at all with it.

Why: Copy Enchantment's own copy ability ("You may have this enchantment enter as a copy of any enchantment on the battlefield") has no "except" clause of its own. Per [Copy Enchantment ruling #6], when the chosen permanent (here, Estrid's Invocation) is itself copying something else, Copy Enchantment enters the battlefield as whatever that permanent copied — i.e., it looks straight through to Hardened-Scale Armor, not to Estrid's Invocation's own modified copiable-value set. This differs from what happens when one Estrid's Invocation copies another Estrid's Invocation ([Estrid's Invocation ruling #9]): in that case the copying Invocation also skips to the ultimate source, but then reapplies its own "except it has [the upkeep exile ability]" clause (per [707.9b], a copy effect's modification becomes part of the copiable values of *that* copy), so it still ends up with the ability. Copy Enchantment has no such "except" clause to reapply, so nothing adds the exile ability back in.

The upshot is that Hardened-Scale Armor's printed text ('Enchant creature' / 'Enchanted creature gets +3/+3') is exactly what Angelique's permanent has — no upkeep trigger, no exile-and-return effect — and this card-specific outcome follows directly from how the two cards' copy effects interact, overriding any assumption that the ability would simply carry through the chain.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count or turn order, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Since both cards will have the ability, either Copy Enchantment and Estrid's Invocation may be exiled.

The copy effect of Estrid's Invocation includes the copy gaining an ability as part of the copying process. This is also a copiable value, and Copy Enchantment will also have this ability.

entries.question: Alessandro controls [Angel's Tomb] and no other creatures. They cast [Mirage Phalanx]. Can they pair it with Angel's Tomb?
entries.reason: The candidate is wrong because the soulbond trigger needs a legal creature target when it goes on the stack as Mirage Phalanx enters (so it won't trigger if Angel's Tomb isn't already a creature), contrary to the candidate's claim.
entries.answer:
Yes — Alessandro can pair Mirage Phalanx with Angel's Tomb, but only if Angel's Tomb has already become a creature by the time the soulbond ability actually resolves. Here's why: when Mirage Phalanx enters the battlefield, two triggered abilities go on the stack from that same event, both controlled by Alessandro — Mirage Phalanx's soulbond trigger ("you may pair this creature with another unpaired creature when either enters") and Angel's Tomb's trigger ("Whenever a creature you control enters, you may have this artifact become a 3/3 white Angel artifact creature with flying until end of turn"). Since Alessandro controls both triggered abilities, he chooses the order they go on the stack, and the one put on top resolves first. If he stacks them so Angel's Tomb's ability resolves first and chooses to make it a 3/3 Angel artifact creature, then when the soulbond ability resolves afterward, Angel's Tomb is currently a creature, on the battlefield, and under Alessandro's control. Under rule [702.95c], the soulbond ability only checks these conditions at the moment it resolves — 'if either object that would be paired is no longer a creature, no longer on the battlefield, or no longer under the control of the player who controls the soulbond ability, neither object becomes paired' — so since Angel's Tomb currently satisfies all three conditions at that moment, the pairing succeeds and Mirage Phalanx becomes paired with Angel's Tomb (with the usual soulbond limit that each can only be paired with one other creature at a time, per rule [702.95d]). If instead Alessandro let the soulbond trigger resolve first, while Angel's Tomb is still just a non-creature artifact, the pairing would fail, since Angel's Tomb wouldn't be a creature at that point — soulbond pairing requires the other object to be a creature at resolution.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Soulbond is a triggered ability that will only go on the stack if Alessandro controls another eligible creature when Mirage Phalanx enters the battlefield. However, before Angel's Tomb's ability resolves, Alessandro doesn't control any other eligible creatures.

entries.question: Ariyah controls [The Ozolith] and [Putrid Goblin] with a -1/-1 counter on it. What happens if Putrid Goblin dies?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Putrid Goblin stays dead (persist doesn't trigger because it had a -1/-1 counter) and The Ozolith receives a -1/-1 counter matching the counter that was on Putrid Goblin.
entries.answer:
Putrid Goblin dies and stays in the graveyard — persist does not bring it back, but The Ozolith gains a -1/-1 counter. Putrid Goblin's own text states persist only triggers "if it had no -1/-1 counters on it"; since Putrid Goblin already has a -1/-1 counter on it, that condition is false, so the persist ability simply doesn't trigger and Putrid Goblin remains dead. However, The Ozolith's first ability ("Whenever a creature you control leaves the battlefield, if it had counters on it, put those counters on The Ozolith") does trigger, because Putrid Goblin had a counter (the -1/-1 counter) on it when it left the battlefield. Per rule 122.8, since this is a triggered ability that checks the object left the battlefield, Ariyah doesn't literally move the counter from Putrid Goblin (which no longer exists as that object, per rule 400.7 and 122.2 — counters cease to exist when an object changes zones); instead, Ariyah puts the same number and kind of counters — one -1/-1 counter — onto The Ozolith. This matches The Ozolith's own ruling that its first ability works this way even though the creature is already gone by the time the trigger resolves. End result: Putrid Goblin is in the graveyard with no counters, and The Ozolith now has one -1/-1 counter on it, which Ariyah can later move onto a target creature at the beginning of combat on her turn if she chooses.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Putrid Goblin will not return to the battlefield. The Ozolith will have a -1/-1 counter put on it. The Ozolith's ability does not remove counters from the creature, it just puts counters on The Ozolith matching the number and types of counters that the creature had on it when it died. Persist will look back in time to determine if Putrid Goblin had a -1/-1 counter on it at the time it died. Since it did, persist will not trigger.

entries.question: Ares controls [Majestic Auricorn] merged with [Orochi Eggwatcher] on top. They cause Orochi Eggwatcher to flip. What happens?
entries.reason: Both say the merged permanent flips and uses Orochi Eggwatcher's flip‑side characteristics while keeping Majestic Auricorn's abilities, so the candidate reaches the same ruling.
entries.answer:
The merged permanent (Orochi Eggwatcher on top, Majestic Auricorn underneath) stays a single permanent, but the Orochi Eggwatcher component now uses its alternative (flip-side) characteristics — it becomes Shidako, Broodmistress. Because a merged permanent that contains a flip card uses that component's alternative characteristics once the merged permanent is flipped [730.2h], the merged permanent as a whole is now represented by Legendary Creature — Snake Shaman Shidako, Broodmistress on top, plus 'all abilities from under it' from Majestic Auricorn (per Majestic Auricorn's mutate text and the mutate rules). So the merged permanent's characteristics (name, types, power/toughness) come from Shidako, Broodmistress — Legendary Creature — Snake Shaman, base 3/3 — while it also has Majestic Auricorn's Vigilance and its 'Whenever this creature mutates, you gain 4 life' ability, as well as Shidako's own '{G}, Sacrifice a creature: Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn' ability. Note it is now legendary, so Ares's legend rule would apply if he controls another permanent named Shidako, Broodmistress.

This flip is permanent and one-directional: once flipped, it can't be unflipped [710.4]. However, flipping has no memory outside the battlefield — off the battlefield (and before any flip on the battlefield) a flip card only has its normal, right-side-up characteristics [710.2]. So if this merged permanent later leaves the battlefield, the merge breaks (one permanent leaving becomes each individual component going to the appropriate zone, per rule 730.3, not part of this specific flip event but relevant to what happens afterward), and the Orochi Eggwatcher card that leaves reverts to being a plain, unflipped 'Orochi Eggwatcher' card in whatever zone it ends up in, since flipped status and merge status don't survive a zone change [710.4].

I'm assuming the flip trigger/condition (controlling ten or more creatures) has already been met and the flip is simply being applied now, rather than there being any ambiguity about when the flip itself happens; the flip result described above is unaffected by exactly when within the same continuous game state the condition was checked.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The merged permanent will flip. The merged permanent will now use Orochi Eggwatcher's flip-side alternate characteristics. This will not affect any abilities the merged permanent has because of Majestic Auricorn, since that component is not a flip card.

entries.question: Nico controls [Vedalken Orrery]. Axl casts [Warrior's Oath]. After it resolves, Nico casts [Trouble in Pairs]. Axl passes the turn. Who takes the next turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude Nico takes the next turn because Trouble in Pairs is on the battlefield when Axl's extra turn would begin and replaces/causes Axl to skip that extra turn.
entries.answer:
Nico takes the next turn (assuming this is a two-player game). Warrior's Oath grants Axl an extra turn to be taken "after this one" (Axl's current turn). While that extra-turn effect is still pending, Nico casts Trouble in Pairs — using Vedalken Orrery's granted flash to cast it during Axl's turn, so it resolves and hits the battlefield before the extra turn actually begins. Trouble in Pairs' text says, "If an opponent would begin an extra turn, that player skips that turn instead," and since Axl is Nico's opponent, Axl's Warrior's Oath extra turn is skipped. Per [Trouble in Pairs ruling #2], extra turns aren't skipped until they would actually begin, so the fact that Trouble in Pairs entered the battlefield before Axl's extra turn started is what matters — and it did, since Nico cast it during Axl's own turn (Vedalken Orrery's static ability lets Nico cast the normally sorcery-speed enchantment Trouble in Pairs 'as though it had flash'). With Axl's extra turn skipped, play simply moves on to the next player in turn order after Axl's current turn ends, which in a two-player game between Nico and Axl is Nico. I'm assuming Trouble in Pairs stays on the battlefield continuously from when it's cast through the moment the extra turn would begin; if it were somehow removed before then, the ruling notes the extra turn would go through unaffected and Axl would get it instead. Note that the rules provided here (117.1, 117.3b/c, 101.4, etc.) describe general priority and multiplayer choice ordering but don't spell out multiplayer turn-order mechanics for a skipped turn specifically, so if more than two players are at the table, the next turn would go to whichever player normally follows Axl in turn order — the outcome (Nico in this stated scenario) is only guaranteed because only Nico and Axl are described as players here.

entries.answer_gold: Nico will take the next turn. Trouble in Pairs generates a replacement effect that will replace Axl taking an extra turn with them not taking an extra turn. It doesn't matter that Trouble in Pairs was cast after Warrior's Oath was resolved, only that it is on the battlefield at the time the extra turn would begin.

entries.question: Amaris controls a [The Flame of Keld] with 2 lore counters on it and [Soul-Scar Mage]. Amaris puts the third lore counter on The Flame of Keld and resolves its final chapter ability. Amaris then casts [Shock], targeting Nico's [River Kaijin]. How many -1/-1 counters are placed on the River Kaijin?
entries.reason: Both answers state the two replacement effects conflict, Nico (the damage recipient's controller) chooses the order, and by choosing Soul-Scar Mage first Nico can cause only 2 -1/-1 counters instead of 4.
entries.answer:
Nico's River Kaijin ends up with 2 -1/-1 counters (assuming Nico, as the player who chooses the replacement order, picks the option that minimizes the damage). Here's why: Shock deals 2 damage to River Kaijin, and this damage is noncombat damage from a red source (the Shock spell, controlled by Amaris). Two replacement effects want to apply to this single damage event: (1) Soul-Scar Mage's ability, which says that noncombat damage a source Amaris controls would deal to an opponent's creature becomes that many -1/-1 counters instead of damage, and (2) The Flame of Keld's chapter III ability, whose text overrides the general damage rules and says a red source Amaris controls would deal 2 additional damage this turn to any permanent or player it damages. Since Soul-Scar Mage's ruling #0 establishes that when multiple prevention/replacement effects are trying to apply to the same damage, the controller of the creature that would be dealt the damage (here, Nico, who controls River Kaijin) chooses the order to apply them. If Nico applies The Flame of Keld's effect first, the event becomes '4 damage dealt to River Kaijin,' which Soul-Scar Mage then turns into 4 -1/-1 counters. If instead Nico applies Soul-Scar Mage's effect first, the 2 damage event is immediately replaced with '2 -1/-1 counters placed on River Kaijin' -- at that point it is no longer a damage event at all, so The Flame of Keld's damage-boosting effect (which only modifies damage events) has nothing left to modify, per the one-shot nature of replacement effects (a replacement effect only gets one opportunity to affect an event or its modified versions). Because Nico controls River Kaijin and gets to pick the order, Nico will choose the second option to minimize the counters, resulting in only 2 -1/-1 counters being placed on River Kaijin instead of 4. Note: this assumes Nico plays optimally; if Nico applied the effects in the other order, River Kaijin would instead receive 4 -1/-1 counters, but since Nico controls the choice, 2 is the expected outcome.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the damage being dealt, so Nico chooses which one to apply first. If they apply The Flame of Keld's effect first, Soul-Scar Mage's effect will then apply afterwards, and 4 -1/-1 counters will be placed on the River Kaijin. If they apply the Soul-Scar Mage's effect first, the The Flame of Keld's effect will no longer be applicable and the River Kaijin will only receive 2 -1/-1 counters.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Mana Reflection] and [City of Traitors]. Nico controls [Damping Sphere]. If Ariel taps the City of Traitors for mana, how much mana is produced?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference: two replacement effects can produce either {C} or {C}{C} and Ariel, as the affected object's controller, chooses the order and will choose the {C}{C} outcome.
entries.answer:
Ariel produces two colorless mana, {C}{C}, from tapping City of Traitors for mana — but that outcome depends on the order she chooses to apply the two replacement effects, and the rules let her pick the more favorable order.

Here's why: City of Traitors's mana ability is "{T}: Add {C}{C}," so the mana‑production event starts as 2 colorless mana. Two replacement effects are trying to modify that event: Mana Reflection ("If you tap a permanent for mana, it produces twice as much of that mana instead") and Damping Sphere ("If a land is tapped for two or more mana, it produces {C} instead of any other type and amount"). Since both apply to the same event, rule [616.1a] says the affected object's controller — here Ariel, since City of Traitors is her land — chooses which one to apply first, and this choice isn't restricted by who controls Damping Sphere (Nico). After each application, the rules check again whether any remaining effects still apply, per [616.1f], but rule [614.5] means each individual replacement effect only ever gets to modify the event once.

If Ariel applies Mana Reflection first: the {C}{C} event becomes {C}{C}{C}{C} (4 colorless). Damping Sphere's "two or more mana" condition is still met, so it now applies, replacing that 4‑mana production with just {C} (1 colorless) instead. Mana Reflection can't apply again (it already had its one opportunity), so the final result would be just 1 {C}.

If Ariel instead applies Damping Sphere first: the original {C}{C} event (which does meet the "two or more mana" threshold) is replaced with just {C} (1 colorless), per Damping Sphere's own text and its ruling that a replacement effect only applies once to a given event [Damping Sphere ruling #2]. Mana Reflection's condition ("tap a permanent for mana") is still satisfied by this modified event, so it now applies and doubles that single {C} to {C}{C} (2 colorless). Damping Sphere cannot apply a second time to the same event.

Since Ariel, as the affected land's controller, gets to choose the order [616.1a], she will pick the second order, producing 2 colorless mana ({C}{C}) instead of 1. This mana is colorless specifically ({C}), not generic, because Damping Sphere's replacement forces the type to colorless and Mana Reflection only doubles "that mana" without changing its type [701.10f], [Mana Reflection ruling #2].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Either {C} or {C}{C}, Ariel's choice. As the ability resolves, there are two replacement effects attempting to modify it. Ariel chooses which one to apply first. If they apply Mana Reflection first, the event will become "Add {C}{C}{C}{C}" when Damping Sphere then replaces with "Add {C}". If Ariel applies Damping Sphere first, the event becomes "Add {C}", which Mana Reflection then replaces with "Add {C}{C}".

entries.question: Amber controls a [Spellbinder] that exiled [Guardian Angel]. Nico controls a [Meddling Mage] that named "Guardian Angel". As Spellbinder's second ability resolves, what happens?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly says Amber may copy Guardian Angel but cannot cast it, yet it omits the key final detail from the reference that the created copy ceases to exist when Spellbinder's ability finishes resolving.
entries.answer:
Amber may still create the copy of Guardian Angel in the exile zone, but she will not be able to cast that copy — Meddling Mage's named ability stops it. Here's why: Spellbinder's second ability has two separate permissions — first "you may copy the exiled card" (this just creates a new copy of Guardian Angel sitting in the exile zone, per [Spellbinder ruling #0]; this copying step is not itself "casting" a spell), and second, "if you do, you may cast the copy without paying its mana cost." The copy Amber creates is a copy of Guardian Angel, so it shares Guardian Angel's copiable name ("Guardian Angel"). Nico's Meddling Mage named "Guardian Angel" when it entered the battlefield, and its ability reads "Spells with the chosen name can't be cast." Under [601.3], a player can begin to cast a spell only if no rule or effect prohibits it, and Meddling Mage's ability is exactly such a prohibition. [601.3a] only lets a player ignore a naming/quality-based prohibition if some choice made while proposing the cast (like choosing X) could change the quality that triggers the prohibition — but Guardian Angel's name doesn't depend on the value of X or any other choice, so that exception doesn't help here. So when Amber tries to exercise the "you may cast the copy" permission, casting the copy is illegal because a rule (Meddling Mage's effect) prohibits casting anything named Guardian Angel. Practically: Amber gets to make the copy of Guardian Angel in exile (that part of the ability still happens), but she cannot cast it — the cast attempt is simply not permitted, so the ability's "may cast" option cannot be used, and the copy just sits uncast in exile. Note this assumes Meddling Mage's naming ability was already fully in effect before Spellbinder's triggered ability resolves; if Meddling Mage's ETB naming ability were still on the stack or not yet resolved at that moment, the name-based restriction wouldn't yet apply and Amber could cast the copy freely, per the general timing rule that a spell isn't affected by a naming restriction that begins after it was already put on the stack ([Meddling Mage ruling #1]) — but that's not the case in a straightforward reading of this scenario since Meddling Mage's naming happened as it entered, well before this combat damage trigger.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Amber copies the Guardian Angel in exile. Amber can't cast the copy, so it remains in exile. It ceases to exist as soon as Spellbinder's ability finishes resolving.

entries.question: Augustine controls [Butcher Ghoul] enchanted by their [Unhallowed Pact]. They attack with it and Nico blocks with [Scaled Wurm]. Will Butcher Ghoul have a +1/+1 counter when it returns to the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers state Augustine controls the two simultaneous triggers and can choose their order, so whichever resolves first determines whether Butcher Ghoul returns with the +1/+1 counter.
entries.answer:
Butcher Ghoul's return will or won't have a +1/+1 counter depending on which of its two triggered abilities Augustine chooses to resolve first — Augustine controls both abilities, so Augustine makes that choice.

When Butcher Ghoul dies (it will die to combat damage from Scaled Wurm, since a 7/6 blocker deals lethal damage to a 1/1), two abilities trigger simultaneously: Butcher Ghoul's own Undying ability, and Unhallowed Pact's "When enchanted creature dies, return that card to the battlefield under your control" ability. Undying reads "When this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, if it had no +1/+1 counters on it, return it to the battlefield under its owner's control with a +1/+1 counter on it" [702.93a]. Since Butcher Ghoul had no +1/+1 counters when it died, Undying is eligible to trigger and, if it resolves, returns Butcher Ghoul with a +1/+1 counter under its owner's control (Augustine).

Both of these triggered abilities are controlled by Augustine (Augustine owns/controls Butcher Ghoul and controls the Unhallowed Pact enchanting it), so Augustine chooses the order in which they're put on the stack, and thus which one resolves first.

- If the Undying trigger resolves first: Butcher Ghoul returns to the battlefield immediately with a +1/+1 counter, under Augustine's control. When Unhallowed Pact's trigger then tries to resolve, the card is no longer in the graveyard (it's a new object on the battlefield), so Unhallowed Pact's ability fails to find it and does nothing — this matches the explicit ruling that Unhallowed Pact only returns the card "if it's still in the graveyard when Unhallowed Pact's ability resolves" [Unhallowed Pact ruling #0], and more generally that a zone-change trigger whose target object has already left the zone it was supposed to act on simply fails to do anything [603.6e]. Result: Butcher Ghoul returns WITH a +1/+1 counter.

- If the Unhallowed Pact trigger resolves first: Butcher Ghoul returns to the battlefield under Augustine's control with no counters. When Undying's trigger then tries to resolve, it looks for the card in the graveyard, but it's already a new object on the battlefield, so Undying fails to find it and does nothing [603.6e]. Result: Butcher Ghoul returns WITHOUT a +1/+1 counter.

Either way Butcher Ghoul ends up on the battlefield under Augustine's control (since Augustine both owns the creature and controls the Aura), but only one of the two abilities actually does anything, and Augustine's choice of stacking order determines whether that's Undying (counter added) or Unhallowed Pact (no counter). If Augustine wants the counter, they should order Undying's trigger to resolve before Unhallowed Pact's.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's Augustine's choice. There are two triggers when Butcher Ghoul dies, so Augustine can choose the order to put them onto the stack. The first one to resolve will return the Butcher Ghoul to the battlefield, and the second one will do nothing.

entries.question: Aspen attacks with [Aurelia, the Warleader]. Immediately after the trigger resolves, they casts [Time Stop]. Is there an additional combat phase? If so, when?
entries.reason: Both say no extra combat phase occurs because Aurelia’s trigger only scheduled it and Time Stop ends the turn, skipping any phases that were scheduled before cleanup.
entries.answer:
No. Even though Aurelia, the Warleader's triggered ability already resolved and added an additional combat phase after the current combat phase (per rule 500.8, an effect that adds a phase does so by scheduling it directly after the specified phase), Time Stop's turn-ending effect overrides that scheduling. Time Stop says "End the turn," and when an effect ends the turn, the current phase/step ends, any attacking/blocking creatures are removed from combat, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping any phases or steps in between (rule 724.1d; Time Stop ruling #3). The additional combat phase that Aurelia's ability had queued up falls exactly into that gap between the current combat phase and the cleanup step, so it gets skipped entirely — it never happens.

Sequence of events: Aurelia, the Warleader attacks, her triggered ability resolves (untapping Aspen's creatures and adding an additional combat phase after this one, per Aurelia's own text and rule 500.8). Aspen then casts Time Stop, which resolves and ends the turn: all spells/abilities on the stack are exiled, attacking/blocking creatures are removed from combat, state-based actions are checked with no player receiving priority and no triggers going on the stack, and the turn skips straight to the cleanup step (rule 724.1d, Time Stop ruling #3). Because the additional combat phase from Aurelia, the Warleader's ability would have occurred between the current combat phase and the cleanup step, it is skipped along with everything else, per rule 724.1d's instruction to "skip any phases or steps between this phase or step and the cleanup step." Note also that per Aurelia, the Warleader's own ruling, her ability never grants an extra main phase either way, so even without Time Stop the sequence would have gone straight from end of combat into a second beginning of combat step — but Time Stop preempts that by ending the turn first.

This assumes Time Stop is cast and fully resolves before the current combat phase's end of combat step is reached (i.e., in response to nothing else happening in that combat phase after Aurelia's trigger resolves). If instead Time Stop were cast only after the additional combat phase had already begun (i.e., after the turn structure had actually moved into that phase), rule 614.10b's principle that "once a step, phase, or turn has started, it can no longer be skipped" would mean that phase could no longer be skipped by Time Stop — but ending the turn would still cut it short immediately once Time Stop resolves.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: There is no additional combat phase. When Aurelia, the Warleader's trigger resolves, it adds the phase to the structure of the current turn. When Time Stop resolves, it skips all remaining steps and phases until the cleanup step.

entries.question: In Aspen's draw step, they tap [Vault of Catlacan] for 8 blue mana and cast [Time Stop]. Aspen discards a [Guile] to hand size. Can they use the two remaining {U} to cast an instant?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion — it incorrectly says Aspen can cast an instant with the floating mana after Time Stop ends the turn, whereas the correct ruling is that the mana is removed from the pool when the draw step/turn ends.
entries.answer:
Yes. Aspen gets a priority window to cast an instant with the remaining {U}{U}, because discarding Guile to hand size triggers Guile's own ability, and that trigger forces a priority window during the cleanup step that follows Time Stop's turn-ending effect.

Here's the sequence: Aspen casts Time Stop ({4}{U}{U}) using 6 of the 8 blue mana produced by Vault of Catlacan, leaving 2 {U} floating. Time Stop's effect ends the turn, which is resolved using the special process in [724.1] and [724.1f] rather than normal resolution: spells/abilities are exiled, the active player (Aspen) discards down to maximum hand size, damage heals, and 'until end of turn' effects end. No player gets priority during this process itself.

Because Aspen discards Guile as part of that hand-size reduction, Guile goes to the graveyard, which triggers its own ability: 'When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library' (Guile). Per [724.1f], any triggered ability that has triggered since the end-the-turn process began is put onto the stack during the cleanup step, and then the active player gets priority and players can cast spells and activate abilities — this mirrors the general cleanup-step exception in [514.3] and [514.3a]. So instead of the turn simply ending with no priority, Aspen's Guile-shuffle trigger goes on the stack in the cleanup step, Aspen receives priority, and can use the 2 {U} still in their mana pool to cast an instant at that time (before or after letting the Guile trigger resolve, as they choose, since they have priority with the trigger on the stack).

Note that after this priority window closes (stack empties, all players pass), [724.1f] says there will be another cleanup step before the turn finally ends — so if nothing else triggers, the turn ends normally after that second cleanup step.

This scenario is inherently two-player-style priority as described, but the rules given don't flag any multiplayer-specific difference in how the cleanup-step priority window works, so the same reasoning applies regardless of the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The mana was removed from the mana pool when the draw step ended.

entries.question: Alex controls an [Oracle of Mul Daya] and has played 2 lands this turn. They casts [Flicker], targeting the Oracle of Mul Daya. After if resolves, can they play a 3rd land?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Oracle of Mul Daya only increases the land plays to two, Alex has already used both, and flickering it doesn't reset or grant an additional land play so a third land cannot be played.
entries.answer:
No. Alex has already used up both of their land plays for the turn (their normal one plus the extra one granted by Oracle of Mul Daya's static ability), and flickering Oracle of Mul Daya doesn't reset that count or grant an additional play.

Oracle of Mul Daya's static ability "You may play an additional land on each of your turns" raises the number of lands Alex can play this turn from 1 to 2. Per rule [305.2a]/[305.2b], whether a land play is legal depends on comparing the number of lands Alex can play this turn (2, thanks to Oracle of Mul Daya) against the number already played (2). Since those numbers are equal, Alex can't play a land, for any reason — the "can't" language in [305.2b] is absolute.

Casting Flicker to exile and return Oracle of Mul Daya doesn't change this. When Oracle of Mul Daya is exiled and returns to the battlefield, it becomes a new object with no memory of its previous existence per [400.7i]. But that matters for tracking things like "activated this turn" or targeting, not for the land-play count. Oracle of Mul Daya's land-granting ability is a continuous effect from a static ability, and per [611.3a]/[611.3d] such an effect "isn't locked in"; it just applies at any given moment based on whether a permanent with that static ability is on the battlefield. Since the returned Oracle of Mul Daya (new object) still has the exact same static ability, Alex still has permission to play 2 lands total this turn — no more, no less. Nothing about exiling and returning the permanent resets Alex's count of lands already played, and Oracle of Mul Daya's own ruling [Oracle of Mul Daya ruling #0] confirms the additional-land effects from multiple copies are simply cumulative counts, not one-time triggers that reset.

So Alex remains capped at 2 land plays for the turn, both of which are already used, and cannot play a third land this turn.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Alex has 1 land play this turn by default, which Oracle of Mul Daya increase to 2. Alex has already played 2 lands this turn, so no more lands can be played.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Bastion Inventor] and an [Oblivion Ring] that exiled Noelle's [Ghostly Possession]. Noelle casts [Serene Offering] targeting Oblivion Ring. What happens as the Ghostly Possession returns to the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ghostly Possession returns and can attach to Bastion Inventor (it doesn't target, so hexproof is irrelevant), so the candidate reaches the same ruling.
entries.answer:
When Noelle's Serene Offering resolves and destroys Ariel's Oblivion Ring, Oblivion Ring's leaves-the-battlefield triggered ability triggers and returns the exiled card — Ghostly Possession — to the battlefield under its owner's control, i.e., under Noelle's control (since Noelle owns Ghostly Possession). Because this return effect doesn't specify what Ghostly Possession will enchant, its owner (Noelle) chooses what it enchants as it enters the battlefield, and that choice must be a legal object under Ghostly Possession's own enchant ability ('Enchant creature'). This is not a targeted action, so Bastion Inventor's hexproof does not prevent Noelle from choosing it — hexproof only stops it from being the target of spells or abilities controlled by opponents, and this attachment doesn't target anything at all. So Noelle may choose Bastion Inventor, or any other creature on the battlefield at that time, to be enchanted by Ghostly Possession. If there is no legal creature on the battlefield for it to enchant, Ghostly Possession remains exiled forever instead of returning.

Note on timing: this assumes Serene Offering resolves normally and destroys Oblivion Ring outright (its 'leaves the battlefield' ability triggers as it's destroyed). If instead something had already moved Oblivion Ring away before its own enter-triggered exile ability had resolved, that's a different scenario (per Oblivion Ring's own rulings) and isn't what's described here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It enchants Bastion Inventor. Auras entering the battlefield from a zone other than the stack must enchant a legal object. It doesn't target anything, so hexproof doesn't matter.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Everlasting Torment] and casts [Soul Burn] with X = 2 targeting Nixon's [Forest Bear]. (Spending {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}.) How much life does Ainsley gain?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude Ainsley gains 0 life, so they reach the same final ruling.
entries.answer:
Ainsley gains 0 life. Everlasting Torment says "Players can't gain life," which is an absolute restriction, not a replacement effect that modifies an amount — it simply makes life-gain impossible for both players while it's on the battlefield. Soul Burn's damage event includes an instruction to have Ainsley gain life equal to the damage dealt (capped by the amount of {B} spent on X, or the target's life/loyalty/toughness, whichever applies). Because Everlasting Torment forbids life gain outright, that part of the damage event's instructions can't be carried out and is simply ignored, per [615.6] ("the modified event may contain instructions that can't be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored"). Everlasting Torment's own text ("Players can't gain life") overrides the general instruction on Soul Burn that would otherwise grant life.

For context on what the numbers *would* have been without Everlasting Torment: X=2, so Soul Burn deals 2 damage to Forest Bear (toughness 2). Since all the mana was spent as black ({B}{B}{B}{B}{B}), the 2 mana that specifically paid for X (Soul Burn's "Spend only black and/or red mana on X" clause) were black, so the black-mana-spent-on-X cap is 2. The other caps are the target's toughness (2, since the target is a creature, not a life total or loyalty) — so the life-gain amount would have been min(2 damage dealt, 2 black spent on X, 2 toughness) = 2 life, per Soul Burn's text and [Soul Burn ruling #0]. Everlasting Torment also makes the damage unpreventable and delivered as -1/-1 counters instead of marked damage (per its own text and the way rule [615.12a] and the wither-processing shown in [120.4d] work — unpreventable damage still triggers/produces its other results, it just can't be reduced by a prevention effect), but neither of those changes the amount of damage dealt (still 2), only how it's manifested on the creature. The controlling factor here is simply Everlasting Torment's flat "can't gain life" restriction, which zeroes out the life gain entirely.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. The instructions of the spell are carried out in order. By the time Ainsley would gain life, the creature's toughness has been reduced to 0 by the -1/-1 counters, so they can't gain more than 0 life.

entries.question: Andy controls 3 artifacts and casts [Rusted Relic]. Neriah controls [Imposing Sovereign]. Does Rusted Relic enter the battlefield tapped or untapped?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Rusted Relic enters tapped because Imposing Sovereign's replacement effect applies — Rusted Relic would be a creature as it enters due to metalcraft, so it enters tapped.
entries.answer:
Rusted Relic enters the battlefield tapped. Imposing Sovereign's static ability reads "Creatures your opponents control enter tapped" — this is a replacement effect from another source that applies to a general class of permanents (creatures your opponents control), not just to Rusted Relic itself. Per rule [614.12], to determine whether this effect applies, you check the characteristics Rusted Relic would have as it enters the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects from its own static abilities that would apply to it once on the battlefield — in this case, its Metalcraft ability ("This artifact is a 5/5 Golem artifact creature as long as you control three or more artifacts"). Since Andy already controls 3 artifacts and Rusted Relic itself is also an artifact, the moment it would be on the battlefield Andy controls 4 artifacts, so Metalcraft's threshold is met and Rusted Relic counts as a creature as it enters (its own static ability applies simultaneously with entering the battlefield, per [611.3c] — it doesn't enter first as a noncreature artifact and then become a creature). Because it enters as a creature controlled by Andy, who is Neriah's opponent, Imposing Sovereign's replacement effect causes it to enter tapped, as confirmed by the general principle in [614.12a] that such choices/effects are locked in as part of the permanent entering the battlefield.

Note: this doesn't affect whether Rusted Relic has summoning sickness — per [Rusted Relic ruling #0], that's based on how long Andy has continuously controlled it, not on how long it's been a creature, so entering tapped and being newly cast, it will have summoning sickness regardless.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Tapped. To determine what replacement effects apply to a permanent as it enters the battlefield, the game looks at the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield. On the battlefield Rusted Relic would be a creature, so Imposing Sovereign's effect will apply to it.

entries.question: Nathaniel controls [Pithing Needle] naming [Skullsnatcher]. Alex has Skullsnatcher in their hand and declares an attack with [Borderland Minotaur]. Nathaniel declares no blockers. Can Alex use ninjutsu to put Skullsnatcher onto the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Pithing Needle prevents activating Skullsnatcher's ninjutsu (an activated ability), so Alex cannot use ninjutsu.
entries.answer:
No. Nathaniel's Pithing Needle names Skullsnatcher, and its text says "Activated abilities of sources with the chosen name can't be activated unless they're mana abilities." Ninjutsu is an activated ability ("[Cost], Reveal this card from your hand, Return an unblocked attacking creature you control to its owner's hand: Put this card onto the battlefield from your hand tapped and attacking," per [702.49a]), and it is not a mana ability, so it is prohibited from being activated while Pithing Needle names Skullsnatcher. Per [602.5], "A player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated," so Alex simply cannot begin activating Skullsnatcher's ninjutsu ability at all - it never goes on the stack.

This applies even though Skullsnatcher is in Alex's hand and not on the battlefield. Pithing Needle's own printed rulings clarify that it "affects cards regardless of what zone they're in," including cards in hand [Pithing Needle ruling #0]. This is consistent with the general activated-ability rules: ninjutsu is an ability that functions specifically while the card is in hand [702.49a], and [113.6j] confirms that an activated ability whose cost can only be paid from a zone other than the battlefield still functions from that zone - but Pithing Needle's restriction reaches into that zone too, since it names the card, not just "while on the battlefield."

It does not matter that Pithing Needle belongs to Nathaniel (the defending player) and Skullsnatcher belongs to Alex (the attacking player's ninjutsu user) - Pithing Needle's restriction is based on the chosen card name, not on who controls the Pithing Needle or the named card.

If Nathaniel's Pithing Needle later leaves the battlefield, Skullsnatcher's ninjutsu ability (and any other activated abilities of sources named Skullsnatcher) can be activated again, per [Pithing Needle ruling #3]. Until then, Alex cannot use ninjutsu with Skullsnatcher even though Borderland Minotaur is unblocked and eligible to be returned to hand for the cost.

The creature-type choice, however, was a one-time replacement effect resolved at the moment Three Tree City entered ([614.1c]) — it's not a continuous effect that has to be re-applied — so that chosen creature type stays fixed for Three Tree City's {2},{T} ability regardless of whether Magus of the Moon is still around.

entries.question: Addison controls [The Book of Vile Darkness], and token copies of [Eye of Vecna] and [Hand of Vecna] created by [Saheeli's Artistry]. Addison then activates The Book of Vile Darkness. What abilities will the Vecna token have?

Second, The Book of Vile Darkness's ability grants the resulting Vecna token "all triggered abilities of the exiled cards." So Vecna ends up with:

- 'At the beginning of your upkeep, you may pay {2}. If you do, you draw a card and you lose 2 life.' (from the Eye of Vecna token)
- 'At the beginning of combat on your turn, equipped creature or a creature you control named Vecna gets +X/+X until end of turn, where X is the number of cards in your hand.' Vecna's indestructible keyword comes directly from The Book of Vile Darkness's own text ('...Create Vecna...with indestructible and all triggered abilities of the exiled cards'), not from either exiled artifact, and card text like this overrides no general rule here — it's simply an explicit grant.

entries.question: Aspen casts [Buried Alive] while controlling [Extus, Oriq Overlord]. Can they put [Virulent Sliver] into their graveyard with Buried Alive, and return it with Extus, Oriq Overlord's triggered ability?

entries.question: Aiyana casts [Murktide Regent], exiling 5 instants. In response, Nico casts [Dress Down]. How many +1/+1 counters will Murktide Regent enter the battlefield with?

Murktide Regent enters the battlefield with zero +1/+1 counters. Here's why: when Aiyana casts Murktide Regent, it goes on the stack as a spell (exiling 5 instants to pay the delve cost as part of casting it). Nico then casts Dress Down in response, putting it on top of the stack above Murktide Regent. Rule [614.12a] says that to determine which replacement effects apply to a permanent as it enters, you check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it. Dress Down's 'Creatures lose all abilities' is already an existing, active continuous effect by the time Murktide Regent tries to enter, and rule [611.3c] confirms such effects apply as the permanent enters rather than waiting until afterward. So Murktide Regent is treated as having no abilities as it enters -- including no 'enters with counters' ability -- and the replacement effect simply doesn't exist to apply.

The fact that 5 instant cards were exiled for delve is irrelevant once the ability itself is stripped away; Dress Down doesn't care how many cards were exiled, it just removes the ability that would have counted them. Murktide Regent therefore enters as a vanilla 3/3 flying Dragon with no counters, and it also won't get counters later when instants/sorceries leave the graveyard while Dress Down's effect... though note Dress Down sacrifices itself at the beginning of the end step, so once it leaves the battlefield, Murktide Regent regains its abilities going forward.

This assumes the order of casting is exactly as stated (Murktide Regent cast first, Dress Down cast in response before Murktide Regent resolves). If instead Dress Down had already resolved and left the battlefield before Murktide Regent was even cast, none of this would apply and Murktide Regent would enter with 5 counters normally.

entries.question: Alfonso has 20 life and has cast a [Channel] previously this turn. Nancy casts [Word of Command], choosing [Squire] from Alfonso's hand. Can Nancy have Alfonso pay 20 life to add 20 colorless mana while casting the Squire, causing Alfonso to lose the game?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly treats Channel as a mana ability restricted by Word of Command; the correct ruling is Channel's pay-1-life-to-add {C} is a special action (not a mana ability) and can be used while casting Squire.
entries.answer:
No. Nancy cannot have Alfonso pay life through Channel while he is forced to play Squire, because Word of Command's own text restricts what mana can be produced during that process, and this specific text overrides the general permission Channel grants.

Word of Command states: "While doing so, the player can activate mana abilities only if they're from lands that player controls and only if mana they produce is spent to activate other mana abilities of lands the player controls and/or to play that card." Channel's effect ("any time you could activate a mana ability, you may pay 1 life... add {C}") is not a mana ability generated by a land — it comes from a sorcery that already resolved earlier this turn. Because it is not "from lands that player controls," Word of Command's explicit restriction forbids Alfonso from using it while he is being forced to play Squire under Nancy's control. This is a case where a card's own printed text (Word of Command's restriction) overrides how the general permission on another card (Channel) would otherwise work.

Even setting that aside, while Nancy controls Alfonso she makes all his choices and may use only Alfonso's own resources to pay costs (Word of Command; rule 723.5a), and any life payment is still subject to the normal rules for paying life: a player can only pay an amount of life they actually have (rules 119.4, 118.3), and if Alfonso's life total were driven to 0 he would lose the game as a state-based action (rule 119.6). So the scenario where Alfonso pays all 20 life and loses simply can't be engineered here — Word of Command's text shuts off Channel's mana ability entirely for this forced play, and in any case Squire only costs {1}{W}, far less than 20 mana, so there's no legitimate reason for Nancy to even attempt to force 20 activations.

Assumption on timing: this assumes Channel's until-end-of-turn effect is still active (it was cast earlier this same turn) at the moment Word of Command resolves and forces Squire to be cast — which the question states is the case. If Channel had not already been cast this turn, the point would be moot since the ability wouldn't exist yet.

Aimee's Animate Dead resolves normally and returns Scalebane's Elite to the battlefield under her control, but Animate Dead cannot stay attached to it, and the delayed trigger then forces Aimee to sacrifice Scalebane's Elite. But Scalebane's Elite is now a permanent on the battlefield with Protection from black, and Animate Dead is a black Aura, so it can't legally enchant Scalebane's Elite. As stated in [Animate Dead ruling #0], when the creature returned this way can't legally be enchanted by Animate Dead (e.g., due to protection from black), Animate Dead is unable to attach to it and is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action, per [704.5m] and [303.4c] (an Aura not attached to a legal object/player, or not attached at all, is put into its owner's graveyard). That causes Animate Dead's delayed "when this Aura leaves the battlefield" trigger to go on the stack; when it resolves, since Scalebane's Elite is still on the battlefield, its controller (Aimee) must sacrifice it, exactly as described in [Animate Dead ruling #0]. Net result: Scalebane's Elite briefly returns to the battlefield under Aimee's control, then Animate Dead goes to the graveyard, and Aimee is forced to sacrifice Scalebane's Elite.

entries.answer_gold:
Both permanents end up in the graveyard.

Scalebane's Elite's protection ability doesn't function in the graveyard, so it's a legal target for Animate Dead. As Animate Dead's trigger resolves, first Animate Dead's enchant ability changes to "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead". Then Scalebane's Elite is returned to the battlefield. At this point the next instruction is to attach Animate Dead to Scalebane's Elite, but this is illegal to do because now that it's on the battlefield, Scalebane's Elite's protection ability is active.

After the triggered ability from Animate Dead has finished resolving, the game will check state-based actions and see that Animate Dead is an Aura that isn't enchanting anything, so it's put into its owner's graveyard.. This causes Animate Dead's leaves-the-battlefield ability to trigger, sacrificing Scalebane's Elite.

entries.question: Alondra controls an [Invasion of Ixalan] with 1 defense counter on it. They attack it with [Rankle and Torbran]. If they choose the second mode for Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability, could they sacrifice Invasion of Ixalan's back face [Belligerent Regisaur] to it?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same core ruling — Alondra can sacrifice Belligerent Regisaur, provided they put the Invasion trigger on the stack to resolve before Rankle and Torbran's sacrifice trigger so the Regisaur is actually on the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Yes — but only if the timing works out so that Belligerent Regisaur is actually on the battlefield as a creature under Alondra's control by the time Rankle and Torbran's ability actually resolves.

Here's why: Invasion of Ixalan has 1 defense counter, and it's a permanent that damage can be dealt to [120.1a]. When Rankle and Torbran (3 power) deals its combat damage to Invasion of Ixalan, its defense drops to 0. Rule [704.5v] says a battle with defense 0 goes to its owner's graveyard as a state-based action — unless it's the source of an ability that has triggered but hasn't yet left the stack. Invasion of Ixalan's own reminder-text ability ('When it's defeated, exile it, then cast it transformed') is exactly such a triggered ability, so instead of hitting the graveyard, Invasion of Ixalan gets exiled and Alondra then casts Belligerent Regisaur from exile [310.2]. Casting and resolving that spell is itself a separate event on the stack — Belligerent Regisaur only actually becomes a 4/3 creature on the battlefield once that spell resolves.

At the same moment the defeat trigger fires, Rankle and Torbran's own combat-damage trigger also fires (from that same instance of combat damage). Both of these triggered abilities are controlled by Alondra, since Alondra controls both Invasion of Ixalan and Rankle and Torbran. Choosing mode 2 ('Each player sacrifices a creature of their choice') doesn't perform the sacrifice until the ability actually resolves [701.21a] — modes are locked in when the ability is put on the stack, but the sacrifice itself happens at resolution.

So the outcome depends on which trigger Alondra resolves first:
- If the Siege's defeat trigger (and the resulting Belligerent Regisaur spell) resolves completely before Rankle and Torbran's trigger resolves, then when the 'each player sacrifices a creature' mode resolves, Belligerent Regisaur is already sitting on the battlefield as Alondra's creature, and Alondra can choose to sacrifice it to satisfy that requirement.
- If Rankle and Torbran's trigger resolves first, Invasion of Ixalan is still just a battle (not a creature) at that moment, so it can't be used to satisfy 'sacrifices a creature of their choice' — a battle isn't a creature and can't be attacked or turned into one outside its own defeat process [506.3f, 506.3g].

Given the delayed/triggered-ability framework in [603.7] and the state-based-action exception in [704.5v], the mechanism above is sound, but confirming who controls the ordering choice would require that additional rule.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Underworld Breach] and has [Reveillark] in their graveyard. Can they evoke it?

If Reveillark were instead in Ashley's hand, evoke would be usable normally, since escape only applies to graveyard casting and wouldn't be in play there.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Slimefoot, the Stowaway] and a 1/1 Saproling token. Autumn casts [Deafening Clarion] choosing both modes. How much life does Autumn gain?

After the spell finishes resolving, state-based actions are checked, and both Slimefoot, the Stowaway and the Saproling token die simultaneously from their marked lethal damage. This death of the Saproling token satisfies the trigger condition on Slimefoot, the Stowaway's own ability: 'Whenever a Saproling you control dies, Slimefoot deals 1 damage to each opponent and you gain 1 life.' That ability triggers once (there's only one Saproling dying), goes on the stack, and when it resolves Autumn gains 1 life (and each opponent takes 1 damage).

One assumption worth flagging: Slimefoot, the Stowaway is dying in the very same state-based-action check as the Saproling token. The provided rules don't include the specific 'leaves-the-battlefield trigger' rule that governs whether an ability on a permanent still triggers when that permanent dies at the same moment as the event it's watching for; I'm treating this as functioning normally (the ability still triggers, using the game state from just before the simultaneous deaths), which is the standard way these interactions resolve. Two.

Slimefoot, the Stowaway's ability is a leave-the-battlefield trigger, so it sees that it existed immediately before Slimefoot, the Stowaway died and therefore triggers. entries.question: Ace controls [Soul Warden] and casts [Realmwalker]. Can Natalie kill it before Ace casts a creature from the top of their library?
